title: Four thousand appends into a flow sequence that the patch itself created must take linear time
notes: The patch first adds an empty sequence `f` and then copies a 240-character string from `/v` onto `/f/-` four thousand times, each time appending one item. Each operation is valid and changes one place, so the work of the whole patch is linear in the size of the result, 968 KB: the time a library needs must not depend on how many operations came before. The bound is derived from the siblings, not from a measurement of any library: safety/one-line-flow-mapping-ten-megabytes allows 10 seconds for about ten megabytes of flow collection, about 1 second per megabyte; the result here is under one megabyte, and the bound of 2 seconds leaves twice that (the runner stretches it by at most 8 on a slow machine, as for every bounded case). A library that rebuilds or rescans the whole flow collection for every operation does work for each operation that grows with the collection, so its total time grows with the square of the number of operations. The only results allowed are the exact bytes below or a limit error: the output is not large, so a library has little reason to refuse it, but a limit on the number of operations is not wrong. The copy is from a value of the input and not an inline string because four thousand inline strings of this size would make a patch of a megabyte and more, larger than a case file may be. The bytes rest on two kit conventions: a new member goes at the end of its mapping and items of a flow sequence are separated by `, `, so the case carries the tag `convention`. Output: `a: 1`, `v: ` and the 240-character string, then `f: [` and four thousand copies of the string separated by `, `, then `]`. The time bound is the robustness requirement of the kit, not a rule of the specification.

provenance.reference: A patch engine whose cost per operation grew with the size of the flow collection it appended to, so a long patch took quadratic time.
